Title: Innovations in the treatment of anaphylaxis: A review of recent data

Authors:
  - Jay A. Lieberman, MD
  - John Oppenheimer, MD
  - Vivian P. Hernandez-Trujillo, MD
  - Michael S. Blaiss, MD

Journal: Annals of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology

Year: 2023

Doi: 10.1016/j.anai.2023.05.033

Article type: narrative_review

Medical specialty: Allergy and Immunology

Language: en

Funding: Bryn Pharma, LLC

Conflicts of interest: Dr Lieberman has received research funding (to institution) from Aimmune, DBV Technologies, Novartis, and Regeneron; advisory fees from ALK-Abelló, Novartis, DBV Technologies, Aquestive Therapeutics, and ARS Pharmaceuticals; DSMB membership for AbbVie and Siolta Therapeutics; and holds editorial roles. Dr Oppenheimer reports consultancy and advisory fees from Aimmune, Amgen, ARS Pharmaceuticals, Aquestive Therapeutics, and GlaxoSmithKline; DSMB membership for AbbVie, AstraZeneca, GlaxoSmithKline, and Sanofi; and is an executive editor. Dr Hernandez-Trujillo reports consultancy fees from Aimmune, ARS Pharmaceuticals, Bryn Pharmaceuticals, CSL, Covis Pharma, DBV Technologies, Kaléo, Pfizer, Sanofi Regeneron, Takeda, and US WorldMeds; and is a spokesperson for Kaléo. Dr Blaiss reports consultancy fees from ALK-Abelló, BELLUS Health, Lanier Biotherapeutics, Merck, Prollergy Corp, Regeneron, and Sanofi; and speaker fees from ALK-Abelló, Merck, Regeneron, and Sanofi.

Condition or topic: Anaphylaxis and innovative epinephrine treatments

Clinical background: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially fatal allergic reaction requiring prompt epinephrine administration. Intramuscular epinephrine via autoinjector (EAI) is the standard outpatient emergency treatment, but barriers such as undercarriage, underuse, needle phobia, and device size lead to delayed administration and increased morbidity. Patients and healthcare professionals desire more convenient, needle-free options to improve carriage and ease of use.

Objectives:
  - To review recent data on innovative nasal and oral epinephrine products under investigation for the outpatient emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.
Study design: Narrative review

Main findings:
  Description: In a pooled analysis of 175 participants across four phase 1 studies, the intranasal epinephrine spray ARS-1 (1 mg) produced a lower maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) than EpiPen 0.3 mg, but resulted in comparable or greater pharmacodynamic responses, including a mean systolic blood pressure Emax of 16.9 mm Hg compared to 18.1 mm Hg with EpiPen, 14.9 mm Hg with Symjepi, and 10.9 mm Hg with manual intramuscular injection.
  Metric: SBP Emax
  Value: 16.9 mm Hg (ARS-1) vs 18.1 mm Hg (EpiPen) vs 14.9 mm Hg (Symjepi) vs 10.9 mm Hg (IM manual)
  Context: ARS-1 integrated analysis of four phase 1 studies

Main findings:
  Description: In a pivotal crossover study, a 13.2 mg intranasal epinephrine dose (BRYN-NDS1C) achieved higher and more sustained plasma epinephrine concentrations than either 0.3 mg EAI or 0.5 mg manual syringe, with plasma levels >100 pg/mL maintained approximately twice as long as with the EAI.
  Metric: Duration >100 pg/mL
  Value: approximately twice as long as with EAI
  Context: BRYN-NDS1C pivotal crossover study

Main findings:
  Description: In a dose-ranging study, a 6.6 mg intranasal epinephrine dose (BRYN-NDS1C) showed a greater mean Cmax than 0.3 mg EAI, with a peak heart rate increase of 33 bpm above baseline versus 20 bpm with EAI.
  Metric: Cmax and HR Emax
  Value: Cmax greater with IN; HR Emax 33 bpm (IN) vs 20 bpm (EAI)
  Context: BRYN-NDS1C dose-ranging crossover study in 25 adults

Main findings:
  Description: AQST-109 sublingual film 12 mg demonstrated a median time to maximum concentration (Tmax) of 12 minutes, faster than 20 minutes for EpiPen 0.3 mg and 50 minutes for intramuscular manual injection, in the EPIPHAST II study.
  Metric: Tmax median
  Value: 12 min (AQST-109) vs 20 min (EpiPen) vs 50 min (IM manual)
  Context: EPIPHAST II crossover study in 24 adults

Main findings:
  Description: In a phase 1/2 study, FMXIN002 nasal powder 3.2 mg under nasal allergen challenge yielded the highest mean Cmax and earliest Tmax among tested modalities, with a pharmacodynamic response similar to that of 0.3 mg EpiPen.
  Context: FMXIN002 phase 1/2 study in 12 adults with seasonal allergic rhinitis

Main findings:
  Description: Hikma's intranasal epinephrine formulations achieved plasma concentrations >100 pg/mL within 5 minutes; the hydroalcoholic 6 mg formulation provided 73% to 126% of the epinephrine exposure of EpiPen 0.3 mg.
  Metric: Relative epinephrine exposure vs EpiPen
  Value: 73% to 126% (6 mg hydroalcoholic)
  Context: Phase 1 crossover PK study in 60 adults with seasonal allergies

Main findings:
  Description: Across the reviewed needle-free products, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles were generally comparable to or more robust than those of standard intramuscular epinephrine delivery, with no serious adverse events reported.
  Context: Summary of multiple studies

Safety results:
  Notable adverse events:
    - Mild and transient adverse events, most commonly nasal discomfort for intranasal products
    - Headache and mild vomiting reported in some studies (e.g., BRYN-NDS1C)
    - No serious adverse events reported across all investigational products

Secondary results:
  - The presence of oral food residue did not meaningfully affect the pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics of AQST-109 12 mg sublingual film, indicating consistent absorption during real-world eating scenarios.

Interpretation: The pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data from nasal and sublingual epinephrine formulations indicate that these novel products achieve plasma concentrations and physiological effects comparable to those of the standard 0.3-mg epinephrine autoinjector or manual intramuscular injection. Some products produce higher peak concentrations, but it is unknown whether this translates into clinical benefit. The comparable or faster time to peak and sustained therapeutic levels suggest that these needle-free options could address barriers to epinephrine carriage and use, potentially enabling earlier administration during anaphylaxis.

Comparison with prior evidence: All reviewed investigational products were compared with the 0.3-mg epinephrine autoinjector and, in some studies, with manual intramuscular injection. The intranasal and sublingual routes demonstrated similar or higher maximum plasma concentrations and comparable time to maximum concentration. Pharmacodynamic responses were similar or more pronounced, and safety profiles were favorable. These findings align with the goal of matching or exceeding the benchmark set by current intramuscular epinephrine delivery.

Clinical implications:
  - Needle-free epinephrine products may lower the threshold for patient and caregiver use by reducing needle fear and device bulk, potentially leading to earlier administration.
  - Higher and more sustained epinephrine plasma levels could offer therapeutic advantages, but the clinical significance of elevated Cmax or prolonged exposure remains unproven.
  - Despite promising pharmacokinetics, the surrogate nature of plasma levels limits direct inference about efficacy in real anaphylaxis episodes.

Practice implications:
  - If approved, these novel epinephrine products could become patient-preferred alternatives to autoinjectors, improving carriage and confidence in emergency treatment.
  - Robust education and training on anaphylaxis recognition and management are still essential, regardless of the delivery device used.
  - Healthcare providers should be aware that current evidence is based on healthy volunteer studies and that real-world performance during anaphylaxis is not yet established.

Limitations:
  - No clinical or real-world studies have been conducted in patients actively experiencing anaphylaxis.
  - Data in pediatric populations are limited.
  - No head-to-head comparisons between different novel products have been performed.
  - Much of the presented data comes from posters or abstracts and has not undergone full peer review.
  - The optimal plasma epinephrine concentration range for treating anaphylaxis is unknown, making pharmacokinetic endpoints uncertain surrogates.
  - Pharmacodynamic mechanisms and their relationship to clinical efficacy are not fully understood.

Strengths:
  - The review provides a comprehensive synthesis of early-phase human data for multiple innovative epinephrine delivery methods.
  - All products consistently demonstrate pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles that are non-inferior or superior to the current standard of care.
  - The data highlight patient-centered advantages, such as smaller size, needle-free administration, and ease of carriage, which align with expressed patient and caregiver preferences.

Open questions:
  - What is the optimal plasma epinephrine concentration and duration of exposure required to effectively reverse anaphylaxis?
  - Do higher Cmax values or prolonged therapeutic levels translate into clinically meaningful benefits (e.g., reduced hospitalizations, mortality)?
  - What causes the observed pharmacodynamic differences between intranasal/sublingual and intramuscular routes?
  - Which pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic parameters are most predictive of real-world treatment success?
  - How will these products perform in patients during actual anaphylactic reactions, where physiological changes may alter absorption and response?

Future directions:
  - Conduct real-world efficacy studies in patients during anaphylaxis, including pediatric and older adult populations.
  - Perform head-to-head comparative trials among novel products.
  - Evaluate patient and caregiver preferences, ease of use, and actual carriage in everyday settings.
  - Investigate age-related differences in pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic responses.
  - Explore cost-effectiveness and impact on healthcare utilization to support widespread adoption.

Main conclusion: There remains a substantial unmet need in anaphylaxis management due to persistent barriers with current EAIs. The investigational needle-free epinephrine products—nasal sprays and sublingual film—exhibit pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles that are comparable to, or in some aspects superior to, those of the standard 0.3-mg EAI and manual intramuscular injection. Their approval may help overcome obstacles such as needle phobia, poor carriage, and delayed administration, potentially improving patient outcomes and satisfaction.

Narrative summary: Current first-line outpatient emergency treatment for anaphylaxis relies on intramuscular epinephrine via autoinjectors (EAIs), but undercarriage and underuse are common due to factors like needle phobia, bulky devices, dosing limitations, and training gaps. This review evaluates human studies on novel nasal and sublingual epinephrine products intended to address these barriers. Data from phase 1 and 2 studies show that several nasal sprays (ARS-1 2 mg, BRYN-NDS1C 13.2 mg, FMXIN002 3.2 mg, Hikma) and a sublingual film (AQST-109-DESF 12 mg) achieve peak plasma concentrations (Cmax) and times to peak (Tmax) comparable to or better than a 0.3-mg EAI. For example, ARS-1 had a mean Cmax lower than EpiPen but produced comparable or greater blood pressure increases; BRYN-NDS1C 13.2 mg yielded higher and more sustained plasma levels than the autoinjector; AQST-109 12 mg showed a faster median Tmax of 12 minutes versus variable EAI times. Pharmacodynamic responses, including heart rate and blood pressure changes, were generally similar or more pronounced. Safety profiles were acceptable, with mild and transient adverse events. Importantly, no studies have been conducted during actual anaphylactic episodes, and pediatric data are sparse. Despite these limitations, the portability, ease of use, and needle-free design of these products could encourage earlier epinephrine administration, potentially reducing morbidity and mortality. FDA approval, which hinges on pharmacokinetic equivalence and safety, may soon expand options for patients and caregivers, alleviating key barriers to effective anaphylaxis management.
